title: Speed Skating Skin Suits: How to Choose a Size, Get the Fit Right and Make It Last
thumbnail_text: Your skin suit is probably the wrong size

scenes.heading: Speed Skating Skin Suits
scenes.sub: Choose the right size, check the fit, make it last
scenes.narration: By the end of this video, you will know how to pick the right skin suit size and how to check the fit properly. You will also know how to wash and store it so it lasts a whole season. The skin suit is the piece of kit skaters think about least and complain about most. On race day, someone is always tugging at a sleeve on the start line. Or they find that a suit which felt fine in the shop cuts into their shoulders the moment they crouch. The reason is simple. A skin suit is not clothing. It is equipment, and it is sized like equipment.

scenes.heading: A skin suit is cut smaller than you
bullets: Normal clothes carry extra room, called ease
A skin suit has negative ease
It stretches onto you, under tension
Your usual size assumes ease
scenes.narration: Your normal clothes are cut with ease. Ease is the extra room a garment carries beyond your body measurement, so it hangs nicely and lets you move. A skin suit works the other way. It has negative ease. It is cut smaller than you, and it stretches onto you. The fabric is meant to be under tension while you wear it. That is why the advice to order your usual size does not help here. Your usual size assumes there is room to spare. Almost everything you know about picking a t shirt size works against you with a race suit.

scenes.heading: Everyday fit versus race fit
scenes.narration: This diagram shows the difference. On the left, everyday clothes are cut larger than your body, with a gap of spare room all around. On the right, the race suit is cut smaller than your body. When you put it on, it stretches and holds itself under tension against you. There is no gap for air to get into, and nothing to flap. Keep this picture in mind whenever you try on a suit. If it feels like normal clothing, it is probably too big.

scenes.heading: Judge fit in your skating position
scenes.chapter: Judge fit in your skating position
scenes.narration: Here is the single most useful idea in this guide. Always judge fit in your skating position. The common mistake looks like this. A skater stands upright in front of a mirror, decides the suit feels tight, and sizes up. Then they get low, and the suit is loose across the back and bunching at the hips. The diagram shows why. A suit that feels comfortable standing is usually too big. A suit that feels snug standing and comfortable in your low position is the one cut for racing. Your position is the shape the suit was patterned for.

scenes.heading: Three checks in position
bullets: Can you breathe fully into your ribs?
Does the crotch seam stay put?
Can you swing an arm across freely?
Tight is fine. Restriction is not.
scenes.narration: So put the suit on and get into your real position. Bend your knees, keep your back flat, chest low, and put your arms where they live when you skate. Now check three things. First, can you breathe fully into your ribs at the bottom of your position? Second, extend one leg fully sideways. Does the crotch seam stay put, or does it drag down? Third, swing an arm across your body. Does the shoulder pull uncomfortably? Tightness is expected. Restricted breathing, or a suit that blocks a full stroke, is not.

scenes.heading: Reading the size run
bullets: Numbers 4 to 16 are junior and youth sizes
Small steps for growing bodies
S, M and L are adult sizes
Bigger steps between adult sizes
scenes.narration: Some suits come in two size runs on one product. The LiveLica Pro Skin Suit, for example, comes in sizes 4 to 16 in steps of two, and also in small, medium and large. The numbers are the junior and youth end of the run. They step in twos because young bodies change quickly, so a small gap between sizes matters. If you are buying for a young skater, this is the run you are working in. Small, medium and large are the adult sizes. The steps between them are larger, which is the usual trade off in adult race kit.

scenes.heading: Should you buy a size up to grow into?
bullets: An oversized suit stops doing its job
No compression, no aerodynamic fit
Leg grippers cannot grip
Buy for the body in the room
scenes.narration: Every parent of a junior skater asks this at some point. Should you buy a size up so the suit lasts longer? It is an understandable instinct, but it is the wrong call for a race suit. An oversized skin suit does not just look loose. It stops doing the job it exists to do. The compression is not compressing. The aerodynamic pattern does not sit where it was designed to sit. And the leg grippers cannot grip a leg they do not reach. A suit bought a size up does nothing useful for a year, then fits for six months. Buy for the body that is in the room.

scenes.heading: What the fabric is doing
bullets: Heavier lycra holds shape and lasts longer
Lighter lycra is cooler and more forgiving
Two way stretch moves with your stroke
Pilling means the fabric is breaking down
scenes.narration: Fabric weight is measured in grams, and it quietly decides how a suit behaves. Lighter fabric is cooler and more forgiving. Heavier fabric holds its shape under load, does not turn see through when stretched in position, and lasts longer before it sags. A good suit uses different weights in different places. Look for stretch in two directions, because your leg extends sideways and backwards at the same time. Fabric that only stretches one way fights you in the other. And watch for pilling. Those little balls of fluff are broken fibres, which means the suit is losing compression and its smooth surface.

scenes.heading: Details that decide race day
bullets: Silicone leg grippers stop the leg riding up
Snug, ribbed sleeves reduce drag
A back zip keeps the front clean
Zip it up with the suit relaxed
scenes.narration: A few details matter on race day. Silicone leg grippers stop the suit leg riding up. Every centimetre it climbs is fabric bunching at your hip, and that bunch creates drag in exactly the wrong place. A laser cut leg edge means no hem, so there is no seam ridge across your thigh. Ribbed sleeves are an aerodynamic choice, so sleeves should fit snug, not loose. The zip sits at the back to keep the front of the suit smooth where the air hits you first. You may need help getting in and out at first. That is normal. Do the zip up while the suit sits relaxed on your shoulders, never while it is stretched, and close it before the suit goes in your bag.

scenes.heading: Making a suit last
bullets: Rinse in cold water straight after skating
Wash cold, inside out, no fabric softener
Never use a tumble dryer
Dry in shade, store flat or loosely folded
scenes.narration: Lycra has three enemies. Heat, chlorine, and time under tension. You control two of them. Rinse the suit in cold water as soon as you can after a session. Dried sweat leaves salt, and salt slowly grinds the stretch fibres down. Wash it cold, inside out, on a gentle cycle or by hand. Never use fabric softener, because it coats the fibres and ruins both wicking and stretch. Never put the suit in a tumble dryer. Heat kills the elastic fibres, and the suit will never recover its shape. Dry it flat or on a hanger in the shade, out of harsh sun. Then store it flat or loosely folded, not stretched over a hanger or balled up in your kit bag.

scenes.heading: Quick answers
bullets: Between sizes? Usually go smaller
Numbness or restricted breathing is too tight
Wear as little as possible underneath
Pilling usually comes from heat or friction
scenes.narration: A few quick answers. If you are between sizes, generally go smaller. A suit that is slightly small still works, and one that is slightly big does not. The exception is breathing. If the smaller size stops you filling your lungs in position, size up. Numbness, pins and needles, or a crotch seam that will not stay put are signs of too tight. Marks on your skin after a session are normal, but not if they are still there an hour later. Under the suit, wear as little as possible, and nothing with seams. If your suit is pilling, look at heat, hot washing, or washing it with zips and velcro.

scenes.heading: Buy for the position, not the mirror
scenes.sub: Full guide at livelica.com, link in the description
scenes.narration: Be realistic about what a suit gives you. It will not add power to your stroke. It stops you losing things, like flapping fabric, shifting kit, chafing and sweat. If you take one thing from this video, make it this. Try the suit on and get into your skating position before you decide anything. The mirror lies, but your position tells the truth. Get the size right, wash it cold, keep it away from the dryer, and a good suit will still be doing its job at the end of the season. The full guide is on the LiveLica blog, and the link is in the description.
